gap_map.why_it_matters: No skill collection published by the Spring team was found on 2026-08-27. This is the largest gap in the registry: Spring Boot is a heavily convention-driven framework, exactly the kind where a framework-team skill pays the most.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor works from the codebase and consults Spring documentation on demand, and states plainly that no framework-team skill is available. If you find one, open an issue - see CONTRIBUTING.md.

gap_map.why_it_matters: @SpringBootTest is the path of least resistance and boots the whole context for every test. Suites built that way get slow enough that people stop running them, which is worse than having fewer tests.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor applies references/quality-gate.md, and pushes tests down to plain unit tests and slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) unless full-context wiring is the thing under test.

layers.name: unit
layers.belongs_here: a service with its collaborators passed in - business rules, plain JUnit, no Spring context
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the test is annotated @SpringBootTest to check one calculation

layers.name: slice
layers.belongs_here: one layer with a minimal context: @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories
layers.cost: moderate; boots a fraction of the context
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: you needed three @MockBean declarations to make the slice start

layers.name: integration (@SpringBootTest)
layers.belongs_here: the wiring: configuration, transactions, real repositories, security filters

layers.name: e2e
layers.belongs_here: flows against a running application, often with Testcontainers

testing.proportions: No proportions stated by the Spring team. The economics set the shape: @SpringBootTest is the path of least resistance and the most expensive, so the slice layer is the one this stack most often skips and most needs.
rules: Reach for plain JUnit first, then a slice annotation, and only then @SpringBootTest. Every step up multiplies the context boot cost across the whole suite.
Use the wrapper that exists in the repository - ./mvnw or ./gradlew - and never both.
Prefer Testcontainers over an in-memory database when the production database is not H2. A suite that only passes against H2 tests a database you do not run.
Assert on behaviour, not on the number of interactions with a mock.
traps: @SpringBootTest everywhere: the suite grows slow enough that people stop running it locally, which is worse than having fewer tests.
@Transactional on a test rolls back at the end, so a bug in commit-time behaviour - flushes, constraints, triggers - never surfaces.
An in-memory H2 database accepts SQL that the production database rejects, and vice versa.
@MockBean replaces the bean in a shared application context, so an unrelated test that reuses that context gets the mock.
Dirty context between tests: @DirtiesContext fixes correctness and destroys suite runtime; both failure modes are silent.
what_not_to_test: That the application context loads - a contextLoads() test proves configuration parses, not that anything works.
Framework behaviour: that @Autowired injected, that Spring Data generated a query method.
Generated Flyway or Liquibase migration files; test the resulting schema instead.
testing.notes: Pick the Maven or Gradle command by which wrapper exists in the repository; never run both. Slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) are the layer this stack most often skips and most needs.

growth_thresholds.extract_service_layer: a controller method exceeds 30 lines, which means business logic has leaked into the transport layer

architecture.pattern: package-by-feature under a root application package

layers.name: root package
layers.holds: the @SpringBootApplication class, above every other class. It defines the base package for component scan, @EntityScan and @ConfigurationPropertiesScan.
layers.must_not: anything else - and never the default package, which makes Spring scan every class in every jar

layers.name: feature package
layers.holds: one domain concept and everything it needs: Customer, CustomerController, CustomerService, CustomerRepository - the layout the Spring Boot docs show

layers.name: Controller
layers.must_not: business rules - a controller method past ~30 lines has absorbed the service

layers.name: Service
layers.must_not: knowledge of HTTP or of the persistence framework

variants.name: Package-by-feature (the Spring Boot docs' own example)
variants.use_when: the default; the reference documentation shows customer/ and order/ packages each holding their own controller, service and repository
variants.cost: a feature package can still grow into a monolith of its own without an enforced boundary

variants.name: Package-by-layer (controller/, service/, repository/)
variants.use_when: a small application, or a team that already works this way
variants.cost: every feature change touches three packages, and nothing stops any service calling any repository

variants.name: Spring Modulith
variants.use_when: domain boundaries need enforcing rather than agreeing - the Spring Boot docs point here explicitly
variants.cost: a dependency and a set of rules the team has to learn and keep passing

rules: Never use the default package. Spring Boot's own documentation calls it out: with @ComponentScan or @SpringBootApplication, every class from every jar gets read.
The main application class sits in a root package above everything else. Its package is the scan base for components, entities and configuration properties.
Package by feature, not by layer. The reference documentation's example is customer/ and order/, each holding its own controller, service and repository.
A controller translates HTTP and delegates. Business rules go in a service that can be tested without MockMvc.
Use reversed-domain package naming (com.example.project), as the documentation states.
architecture.component_library: Not applicable. Shared behaviour moves to a package both features depend on, at >=2 consumers.
architecture.notes: Verified against the Spring Boot reference documentation. It also points at Spring Modulith for teams that need domain boundaries enforced rather than agreed.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Maven and Gradle are both first-class, and the wrapper committed to the repository decides it for everyone.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Whatever the team and the organisation already run.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Switching later rewrites the build, the CI pipeline and every developer's muscle memory.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Spring Data JPA, JDBC and jOOQ are all supported and produce very different code.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Spring Data JPA for domain-shaped data; JDBC or jOOQ when the queries are the product.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: JPA's lazy loading and identity semantics leak into the service layer, so replacing it later is not a swap.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Spring imposes nothing, and the argument is as old as the framework.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Package-by-feature: it is what the Spring Boot reference documentation shows.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Package-by-layer makes every feature change a three-package edit and lets any service reach any repository.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Spring Security is powerful and defaults to locking everything; the policy is yours.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Decide once, and make each endpoint's authorization decision explicit including 'permitAll on purpose'.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A misread security config either exposes an endpoint or blocks a working one, and both look like configuration noise.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Nothing forces a choice, and the cheap option diverges from production.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Testcontainers when production is not H2.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A suite green against H2 gives no evidence about the database you actually deploy against.

operability.observability: Spring Boot Actuator exposes health and metrics, and Micrometer is the instrumentation seam. A @ControllerAdvice handler is where an unhandled exception becomes a recorded, shaped error instead of a bare 500.
operability.authorization: Spring Security, via method security or URL rules. An endpoint with neither is public, and looks exactly like one that is public on purpose.
done_checks: the application boots with the production profile
clean clone and build from scratch
rules: Every endpoint states its authorization decision, including 'public on purpose'.
Every outbound client has a connect and a read timeout. A RestTemplate with no timeouts waits indefinitely and exhausts the thread pool.
A @ControllerAdvice handler reports unhandled exceptions. Without one they become 500s with no record.
Configuration is validated at startup with @ConfigurationProperties and validation, so a missing value fails the deploy rather than the first request.
Schema changes ship as versioned, reversible migrations. Never rely on ddl-auto in anything past a prototype.

dead_code_risks: Beans instantiated by component scan and never imported by name
Classes referenced only from application.yml or application.properties
JPA entities discovered by package scan
Anything reachable only by reflection, including Jackson serialization targets
Flyway or Liquibase migration files discovered by directory scan
Beans activated by a @Profile or @ConditionalOnProperty that is currently off
